intro: Kimiko Ishizaka plays the fugue that closes Book I of The Well-Tempered Clavier. Its subject touches all twelve notes of the chromatic scale, twisting through semitones before four voices gradually crowd the keyboard.

sections.label: A · Alto, tenor, bass, then soprano
sections.mNote: Four voices take up the chromatic subject in turn

sections.label: B · Descending bass, returning alto
sections.mNote: Short imitations separate the complete subject entries

sections.label: A′ · The tenor in E minor
sections.mNote: The subject moves into new keys and closer imitation

sections.label: A″ · Four voices crowd together
sections.mNote: Subject beginnings arrive one bar apart

sections.label: C · Running notes towards F♯ minor
sections.mNote: Semiquavers prepare the tenor’s next entry

sections.label: B′ · The tenor supplies the bass
sections.mNote: Soprano and alto exchange figures above the tenor

sections.label: Coda · A low F♯ holds
sections.mNote: The alto recalls the subject above the dominant pedal

sections.label: D · B major under a fermata

cues.title: Alto, all twelve notes
cues.text: After a short rest, the alto begins F♯–D–B. Wide leaps connect pairs of notes only a semitone apart. Before this long subject finishes, it has touched all twelve notes of the chromatic scale; the line settles on F♯, ready for an answer.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 1–4, alto; Mutopia edition, https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The bass takes the subject
cues.text: The bass states the subject in B minor, F♯–D–B again, now in the lowest voice. Above it the tenor descends B–A–G♯–F♯ in crotchets, while the alto keeps a quicker line of dotted notes and semiquavers. Three speeds sound at once.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 9–12: bass subject, tenor crotchets B–A–G♯–F♯ in bar 10, alto dotted-quaver and semiquaver figures. Mutopia edition (LilyPond source, notes.lyi), music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The soprano arrives last
cues.text: The subject reaches the highest voice after its turns in alto, tenor and bass. Under the soprano’s F♯-minor answer, the bass takes a slower descending line. Each part inherits a job another voice has just finished.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 1–16: entries in alto, tenor, bass and soprano; descending countersubject in the bass at bars 13–16. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The bass steps down
cues.text: The bass descends through short four-note patterns. Above it, soprano and tenor pass a quicker figure between them, holding notes across the beat. The alto briefly remembers the subject’s first three notes, then leaves the other voices to continue.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 17–20: descending bass sequence, soprano–tenor imitation and alto fragment in bar 19. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The alto, between its companions
cues.text: After the episode the alto brings back the complete subject, F♯–D–B, in B minor. Above it the soprano descends B–A–G♯–F♯ in crotchets, the same countersubject the tenor sang in bar 10. The subject lies in an inner voice.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 21–24: alto subject F♯–D–B–G–F♯–B–A♯, soprano crotchets B–A–G♯–F♯ in bar 22. Mutopia edition (LilyPond source, notes.lyi), music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The tenor has the subject
cues.text: B–G–E: the tenor begins the subject in E minor. The bass sounds E and falls silent, leaving room around the new entry. Above it, the soprano descends in slower notes while the tenor works through the familiar semitone pairs.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 30–33: tenor subject, bass rest after E and soprano countersubject. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A singer in the household
cues.text: On 3 December 1721 Bach marries Anna Magdalena Wilcke, a court singer at Köthen. He is Prince Leopold’s music director. The next year, the date on Book I of The Well-Tempered Clavier, he begins looking for a new post.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig chronology, 1717 and 1721 entries, for the appointments, marriage and 1722 job search: https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology. Book I’s autograph title page is dated 1722.

cues.title: Four entries, one bar apart
cues.text: The soprano begins in B minor; a bar later the alto starts in E minor. The bass follows in A major, then the tenor in D major. The voices cut across one another before the subject can finish: this crowding of entries is called stretto.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 41–47. Entry order and keys also tabulated at https://tonic-chord.com/bach-prelude-and-fugue-no-24-in-b-minor-bwv-869-analysis/.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The tenor in F♯ minor
cues.text: The tenor begins C♯–A–F♯, carrying the subject into F♯ minor. Its winding continuation needs B♯ and even F𝄪. The soprano moves in longer notes above it, giving the restless tenor something slow to lean against.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 53–56: tenor entry in the second half of bar 53, B♯ and F𝄪 in bar 55. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: B minor is home again
cues.text: After the entries in F♯ minor and E major, the tenor starts F♯–D–B late in the bar, and B minor is home again. Soprano and alto carry on with their own tied notes and running figures above it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 53–63: tenor entries in F♯ minor (bar 53) and bass entry in E major (bar 57), then tenor F♯–D–B late in bar 60. Mutopia edition (LilyPond source, notes.lyi), music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The bass stays silent
cues.text: Soprano and alto exchange the episode’s quick figures. The bass voice rests, so the tenor supplies the line beneath them, stepping down through the same small patterns heard earlier. The music is gathering itself for the final low-voice entries.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 64–70: soprano–alto imitation, tenor sequence, bass re-entry in bar 70. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: F♯ holds beneath the alto
cues.text: The bass holds F♯ while the alto gives one last F♯–D–B, the subject’s opening. The low note is a dominant pedal, delaying the arrival on B. Above it, a sustained B rubs against the harmony before resolving to A♯.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 74–75: bass F♯ tied across the bar line, alto subject fragment and soprano B–A♯ suspension. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: D♯ in the last chord
cues.text: The four voices meet on B major. D♯ replaces the D♮ of the home key: the raised final third known as a Picardy third. After all those twisting lines, the score ends with a held chord and a fermata.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bar 76: B–D♯–F♯, with fermatas in the outer voices. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The bass descends beneath tied notes
transitions.from: A · Alto, tenor, bass, then soprano
transitions.how: After the soprano’s answer, the bass descends in repeating four-note groups. Soprano and tenor trade tied notes and semiquavers above it. The soprano’s E hangs over a bass D before resolving down; at the end of the sequence, A♯ in the bass rises to B and the alto restores the complete B-minor subject.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 17–21: bass sequence, soprano suspension across bars 19–20 and alto entry in bar 21. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.

transitions.title: D♯ leads the bass to E
transitions.to: A′ · The tenor in E minor
transitions.how: The bass’s descending sequence ends on D♯, which rises to E. Then the bass stops. The tenor begins B–G–E, the complete subject in E minor, while the soprano supplies its slower descending companion. A three-note hint in bar 28 has become a full statement.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 28–33: tenor fragment, bass D♯–E and tenor subject. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.

transitions.title: Running notes prepare F♯ minor
transitions.to: C · Running notes towards F♯ minor
transitions.how: The D-major entries lead into running semiquavers. The soprano climbs from D, and the alto answers with a similar figure from E. E♯ then appears in the alto, pointing towards F♯ minor. The bass descends A–G♯–F♯ and stops; the tenor begins the next subject later in the same bar.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 50–53: upper-voice runs, alto E♯ and tenor entry after the bass withdraws. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.

transitions.title: The tenor carries the low line
transitions.from: C · Running notes towards F♯ minor
transitions.to: B′ · The tenor supplies the bass
transitions.how: With the bass voice silent, the tenor takes the descending sequence. Soprano and alto exchange the earlier episode’s tied notes above it. The tenor’s final A♯ rises to B before recalling the B-minor subject; the bass then enters underneath in E minor, so the two low voices overlap.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 64–70: tenor sequence and shortened subject, then bass entry. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.

transitions.title: The last chord turns major
transitions.to: D · B major under a fermata
transitions.how: The bass climbs chromatically to F♯ and holds it beneath the alto’s last subject fragment. The soprano’s B resolves to A♯, then rises to B as the bass moves F♯–B. In the alto, E falls to D♯. That raised third makes the final chord B major, held beneath a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 73–76: chromatic bass ascent, dominant pedal, soprano suspension and final B-major chord. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.

composer.epithet: He supplied Leipzig’s churches with music for twenty-seven years and left keyboard players enough work for a lifetime.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, turned up in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. His cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, already makes two people say different things together: one sings the psalmist’s plea, another a hymn in long notes above it.
